branch.title: Standard Model Epistemic Graph
branch.notes: Edges: s2m, m2o (pred/fit/frame/cand), m2s back-edge, m2m lineage; AND routes with (sector, n) and (group, n) legs. Generic layer edges (from/to the whole state layer) are expanded to one route per state node and flagged generic.

extra.sub: rays |ψ⟩; no particle-number degree of freedom
extra.desc: A state is a ray in a separable Hilbert space H_{1}. The space describes exactly one particle: there is no operator in the one-particle framework whose eigenvalue is a particle number.

extra.sub: massless; little group ISO(2), helicity ½

extra.desc: Fock sector built on the electron UIR. The Dirac field ψ_{e} annihilates e^{−} and creates e^{+}, so the N-particle nodes count electrons and positrons together.
Proton sector (Rutherford 1919). Treated as elementary in Fermi's theory; replaced by quark sectors at Step 9 (the proton is a bound state of the strong sector, which is outside this graph).
Neutron sector (Chadwick 1932). Replaced by quark sectors at Step 9.
Neutrino sector as assumed from Pauli (1930) to 1962: a single massless species. Detected by Cowan & Reines (1956). Split into ν_{e} and ν_{μ} at Step 7.
Photon sector: the quantized radiation field A_{μ} of Dirac (1927). Bosonic ladder: symmetrized N-photon states.
Muon sector (Neddermeyer & Anderson 1937). Shown not to be Yukawa's strongly interacting meson by Conversi, Pancini & Piccioni (1947).
Electron-neutrino sector. In the SM as drawn it is massless and left-handed only (no right-handed state), which is what blocks a mass term at Step 11.
Muon-neutrino sector, distinguished from ν_{e} by Danby et al. (1962): neutrinos from π→μν produce μ, not e.
Up-quark sector (Gell-Mann 1964; Zweig 1964; point-like constituents seen in deep inelastic scattering, SLAC 1969). Colour and the gluon sector are not drawn.
Down-quark sector. In the charged current it enters as the Cabibbo-rotated combination d' = cos θ_{C} d + sin θ_{C} s (Cabibbo 1963).
Charged weak boson sector, M_{W} ≈ 80.4 GeV. First observed at the CERN SPS collider (UA1, UA2, 1983).
Neutral weak boson sector, M_{Z} ≈ 91.19 GeV (UA1/UA2 1983; LEP precision 1989–2000).
Higgs-boson sector, m_{H} ≈ 125 GeV (ATLAS, CMS 2012). The scalar doublet Φ has one physical excitation after three components are absorbed by W^{±}, Z.

Time evolution is a strongly continuous one-parameter unitary group generated by the Hamiltonian (Stone 1932). It maps H_{1} onto H_{1}: the back-edge to the state layer. Particle number is conserved by construction.

nodes.label: Observable postulate: Â = Â^{†}, Born rule

extra.desc: Every self-adjoint operator on H_{1} is an observable; its spectrum lists the possible outcomes and the Born rule gives their probabilities (von Neumann 1932). This node sends one edge to each Hermitian operator in the observable layer.

The one-particle Lagrangian fixes the Hamiltonian and therefore both the evolution U(t) and the energy spectrum (e.g. E_{n} = −13.6 eV/n^{2} for hydrogen). Replaced by relativistic wave equations at Step 2 and by the free-field Lagrangian at Step 4.

nodes.label: Quantum field on Fock space (a, a^{†})

extra.sub: φ(x) = Σ_{p}(a_{p}u_{p} + a_{p}^{†}u_{p}^{*}); L_{0} of free fields
extra.desc: The field is the operator that adds or removes one quantum of a given UIR. The Fock space of a species is ⊕_{N} Sym^{N}H_{1} (bosons) or ⊕_{N} Λ^{N}H_{1} (fermions) (Fock 1932); spin–statistics proved by Fierz (1939) and Pauli (1940). The free Lagrangian L_{0} = ψ̄(iγ·∂ − m)ψ − ¼F_{μν}F^{μν} + … reproduces the UIR wave equations. With L_{int} = 0 the S-matrix is 1: no transitions.

extra.sub: minimal coupling of the quantized fields; e(1) ∧ γ(1)
extra.desc: Minimal coupling p → p − eA applied to the quantized fields gives the single interaction term −e ψ̄γ^{μ}ψA_{μ}. One vertex changes N_{γ} by ±1 and N_{e} by 0 (scattering) or ±2 (pair creation/annihilation). Renormalized to all orders by Tomonaga, Schwinger, Feynman and Dyson (1946–49). At Step 9 it is identified as the electromagnetic part of the SU(2)_{L}×U(1)_{Y} gauge interaction with e = g sin θ_{W}.

extra.sub: four fermions at one point; n(1)∧p(1)∧e(1)∧ν̄(1)
extra.desc: Fermi copied the structure of the QED vertex: a nucleon current in place of the electron current and the created pair (e, ν̄) in place of the emitted photon. Gamow & Teller (1936) added axial-vector/tensor terms for ΔJ = 1 transitions. G_{F} ≈ 1.166×10^{−5} GeV^{−2} is dimensionful; the amplitude grows like G_{F}s and partial-wave unitarity fails at √s of order a few hundred GeV (textbook argument), so the node cannot be fundamental.

extra.sub: same G_{F} as β decay: universal Fermi interaction
extra.desc: A second four-fermion node for μ → e ν̄_{e} ν_{μ} and for μ capture. The decisive fact is that one constant fits β decay, μ decay and μ capture (Puppi 1948; Klein 1948; Tiomno & Wheeler 1949; Lee, Rosenbluth & Yang 1949). τ_{μ}^{−1} = G_{F}^{2}m_{μ}^{5}/192π^{3} (with small corrections) makes τ_{μ} the most precise source of G_{F}.

extra.sub: J^{μ} = Σ ψ̄γ^{μ}(1−γ^{5})ψ′; one node for β, μ decay, μ capture
extra.desc: Feynman & Gell-Mann (1958) and Sudarshan & Marshak (1958) replaced the two contact nodes by one current–current term with vector-minus-axial currents. It fixes the Michel parameter ρ = ¾, the neutrino helicity −1 and the parity-violating asymmetries. The hadronic current carries |g_{A}/g_{V}| ≈ 1.27 and, after Cabibbo (1963), cos θ_{C}. Still dimensionful: an effective node.

nodes.label: Charged-current gauge vertex (g/√2) W^{+}_{μ} J^{μ}_{CC} + h.c.

extra.desc: W exchange replaces the contact term. For q^{2} ≪ M_{W}^{2} the propagator reduces to 1/M_{W}^{2} and the V−A node is recovered with G_{F}/√2 = g^{2}/(8M_{W}^{2}): the effective node is the low-energy limit of this one (Weinberg 1979). Renormalizable in the spontaneously broken gauge theory ('t Hooft 1971; 't Hooft & Veltman 1972).

extra.sub: J^{μ}_{NC} = Σ f̄γ^{μ}(T^{3}P_{L} − Q sin^{2}θ_{W})f; predicted 1961–67
extra.desc: The gauge group contains a neutral generator besides the photon; the Z couples to every fermion with strength fixed by T^{3}, Q and one new parameter sin^{2}θ_{W}. Observed by Gargamelle (1973), ten years after the prediction, and measured precisely at LEP/SLC.

nodes.label: Gauge self-interactions ⊃ WWγ, WWZ, WWWW, WWZZ

extra.desc: The field strength of a non-abelian gauge field contains cubic and quartic terms (Yang & Mills 1954). In SU(2)_{L}×U(1)_{Y} they fix the trilinear WWγ and WWZ couplings, tested through e^{+}e^{−} → W^{+}W^{−} at LEP2 (1996–2000).

A scalar doublet with vacuum value v breaks SU(2)_{L}×U(1)_{Y} → U(1)_{em}; three components become the longitudinal W^{±}, Z. The gauge-boson masses and the HWW, HZZ couplings follow from the same term, so the W and Z mass edges of Step 9 are now derived here (Englert & Brout 1964; Higgs 1964; Guralnik, Hagen & Kibble 1964; Weinberg 1967).

nodes.label: Yukawa couplings −y_{f} Φ f̄_{L}f_{R} + h.c. → m_{f} = y_{f}v/√2

extra.sub: H(1)∧f(2); one y_{f} per massive fermion
extra.desc: Gauge symmetry forbids direct masses for chiral fermions; the Yukawa term gives m_{f} = y_{f}v/√2 and an Hf̄f vertex proportional to m_{f}. The y_{f} are free parameters: the mass edges are calibrations, while the pattern of H → ττ, bb̄ rates relative to the gauge channels is a prediction.

The potential fixes v^{2} = μ^{2}/λ and the physical scalar mass m_{H}^{2} = 2λv^{2}. The measured m_{H} fixes λ ≈ 0.13 (calibration); the trilinear coupling λ_{HHH} is then predicted but not yet measured, only bounded by di-Higgs searches.

nodes.label: Candidate: ν mass term (LΦ)(LΦ)/Λ or ν_{R} Yukawa

extra.desc: Two repairs are available in the literature. (i) The dimension-5 operator (LΦ)(LΦ)/Λ uses only existing sectors and gives Majorana masses m_{ν} ~ v^{2}/Λ (Weinberg 1979). (ii) New right-handed sectors ν_{R} with Dirac Yukawa couplings, possibly with Majorana masses M_{R} (seesaw: Minkowski 1977; Gell-Mann, Ramond & Slansky 1979; Yanagida 1979; Mohapatra & Senjanović 1980). Current data do not decide between them (Dirac vs Majorana nature untested).

nodes.label: Gauge–fermion term Σ f̄ iγ^{μ}D_{μ} f ⊃ EM, CC, NC vertices

extra.sub: D_{μ} = ∂_{μ} − igT^{a}W^{a}_{μ} − ig′YB_{μ}; e = g sinθ_{W}
extra.desc: One term of the SM Lagrangian, written with the covariant derivative of SU(2)_{L}×U(1)_{Y}. Expanding D_{μ} gives exactly three vertex types: the electromagnetic vertex (Step 5), the charged current (Step 9) and the neutral current (Step 9). The three effective nodes of Steps 6–8 sit inside this cluster because the charged-current member reproduces them at q^{2} ≪ M_{W}^{2}; the matching condition G_{F}/√2 = g^{2}/8M_{W}^{2} is the lineage edge.

extra.sub: non-abelian part ⊃ WWγ, WWZ, WWWW, WWZZ, WWγγ, WWZγ
extra.desc: The Yang–Mills field strength contains the cubic and quartic self-couplings of the W and Z. No effective node was ever written for these vertices; they were predicted and then tested (LEP2).

extra.sub: → M_{W}, M_{Z}; HWW, HZZ, HHWW, HHZZ
extra.desc: The gauge-covariant kinetic term of the scalar doublet. With ⟨Φ⟩ = v/√2 it produces the W and Z masses and the Higgs–gauge vertices.

extra.sub: → m_{f} = y_{f}v/√2; H f̄ f vertex ∝ m_{f}/v
extra.desc: The only SM term that distinguishes the fermion generations; its couplings are inputs (calibration edges).
Fixes the vacuum value and the Higgs mass; the self-couplings it predicts are the least tested part of the model.

nodes.label: Beyond the SM: candidate ν-mass term

extra.sub: not established; the only cluster with no confirmed member
extra.desc: Holds the candidate repairs for the neutrino-oscillation observable. It is drawn dashed because none of its members is established.

extra.sub: spectrum ℝ; de Broglie p = ħk

extra.desc: The discrete spectra observed since Balmer (1885) are the eigenvalues of Ĥ; Schrödinger (1926) derived the hydrogen levels. Dirac (1928) adds the fine structure. Observed first, explained later: anomaly-driven.
Spin was observed (Stern–Gerlach 1922) and postulated (Uhlenbeck & Goudsmit 1925) before Pauli (1927) and Dirac (1928) gave it a place in the formalism: anomaly-driven.
In the Poincaré-covariant theory mass is the eigenvalue of the Casimir operator P^{2}; it labels the representation rather than being a dynamical variable.
The Pauli–Lubański Casimir gives spin for m > 0; for m = 0 the invariant is the helicity. Both are representation labels.

extra.sub: γ emission/absorption; β decay; e^{+}e^{−} pair creation
extra.desc: (i) Emission and absorption of light, Einstein A and B coefficients (1917). (ii) β decay with a continuous electron spectrum (Chadwick 1914; Ellis & Wooster 1927); the electron is not a nuclear constituent. (iii) e^{+}e^{−} pairs created by γ rays (Anderson 1933; Blackett & Occhialini 1933). In each case the final state has a different number of particles than the initial one, which no node acting within H_{1} can produce.

The generic transition-rate observable. Dirac (1927) derived the rate formula later called Fermi's golden rule. Without an interaction term the rate is zero, so this family stays unexplained until Step 5.
The generic scattering observable, defined through S-matrix elements (Wheeler 1937; Heisenberg 1943; Dyson 1949). S = 1 for the free field.

Compton (1923) measured the wavelength shift and intensity; the Klein–Nishina formula (1929), the first QED cross section from the Dirac equation, reproduces the angular distribution and the high-energy fall-off.

Dirac's hole theory (1930–31) implied an anti-electron; Anderson (1933) and Blackett & Occhialini (1933) observed it. The Bethe–Heitler cross section (1934) in the field of a nucleus follows from the QED vertex at order α^{3}.
Kusch & Foley (1948) found g = 2(1.00119 ± 0.00005). Schwinger (1948) computed the one-loop value α/2π. Today a_{e} is known to ~10^{−13} and agrees with the five-loop QED calculation (PDG).

Lamb & Retherford (1947) measured a splitting of about 1000 MHz that the Dirac equation sets to zero; Bethe (1947) obtained ≈1040 MHz from the electron self-energy with a nonrelativistic cut-off. The modern value is 1057.8 MHz.

extra.sub: fixes the vertex coupling e · parameter
extra.desc: The coupling in the QED vertex is not predicted; α is measured (today most precisely from a_{e} and atom-recoil experiments) and fixes e. Calibration edge.

extra.sub: continuous e spectrum; Kurie plot 1936 · Γ-type
extra.desc: Chadwick (1914) found the β spectrum continuous; Ellis & Wooster (1927) showed the energy is really missing. Fermi's node gives the rate and the shape (Kurie et al. 1936) from phase space × |M|^{2}.
Free-neutron decay n → p e ν̄ was expected once m_{n} > m_{p} + m_{e} was established (Chadwick & Goldhaber 1935) and first measured by Robson (1951). Current value 878.4 ± 0.5 s (PDG 2024).

extra.sub: fixed by τ_{μ} (and 0^{+}→0^{+} β decays) · parameter
extra.desc: The strength of the contact term is an input. From Step 9 on it is a derived combination g^{2}/(4√2 M_{W}^{2}), but still fixed by measurement (τ_{μ}).
The muon itself was unexpected (1937). Its lifetime, ~2.2 μs, is reproduced by the contact node with the β-decay value of G_{F}: the universality signal.

extra.sub: shape of e spectrum in μ decay
extra.desc: Michel (1950) parametrized the electron spectrum of μ decay by ρ; the measured ρ = 0.7518 ± 0.0026 (PDG) agrees with the V−A value ¾.

extra.sub: ν beam from π → μν gives μ, not e (Danby et al. 1962)
extra.desc: Pontecorvo (1959) and Schwartz (1960) proposed the test; Danby et al. (1962) found that neutrinos from pion decay produce muons but no electrons. The observable is about the state layer: the ν sector is two sectors with separate currents (lepton-family conservation).

extra.sub: Wu et al. 1957; Garwin, Lederman & Weinrich 1957
extra.desc: Lee & Yang (1956) noted parity was untested in weak processes and proposed experiments. Wu et al. (1957) found the e^{−} emission of polarized ^{60}Co anti-correlated with the nuclear spin; Garwin et al. (1957) found the μ-decay asymmetry. A parity-conserving node cannot produce a pseudoscalar correlation ⟨J⟩·p_{e}.
Measured through the circular polarization of the γ following K capture in ^{152}Eu. The result −1 is the V−A prediction (left-handed neutrino).
Hasert et al. (1973) observed ν_{μ}N → ν_{μ}X events (no outgoing muon) and one ν̄_{μ}e → ν̄_{μ}e event in the Gargamelle bubble chamber. The NC/CC ratios fix sin^{2}θ_{W}.

Predicted from G_{F}, α and sin^{2}θ_{W}: M_{W}^{2} = πα/(√2 G_{F} sin^{2}θ_{W}) at tree level (≈78 GeV), ≈80.4 GeV with radiative corrections. Observed at the SPS in 1983. PDG 2024 average 80.369 ± 0.013 GeV (CDF 2022 value excluded from the average).
Tree-level relation M_{Z} = M_{W}/cos θ_{W}; observed in 1983 (UA1, UA2) and measured to 2 MeV at LEP.

extra.sub: parameter · fixed by NC data, then M_{W}/M_{Z}
extra.desc: The one new parameter of the neutral current. Calibration edge: measured, not predicted.

The Z line shape gives the invisible width, i.e. the number of light neutrino sectors coupling to the Z: 2.9840 ± 0.0082 (LEP EWWG 2006). A model-layer prediction about the number of state-layer sectors.
The cross section involves ν exchange and the WWγ, WWZ vertices; the gauge cancellation between them is required for unitarity and was confirmed at LEP2.
Existence predicted in 1964; discovered 2012. The value is an input that fixes λ = m_{H}^{2}/2v^{2} ≈ 0.13 (PDG 2024: 125.20 ± 0.11 GeV).

nodes.label: Higgs rates σ×BR: γγ, ZZ^{*}, WW^{*}, ττ, bb̄

extra.desc: Production (gluon fusion, vector-boson fusion, VH) and decay rates relative to the SM expectation; all measured signal strengths are consistent with 1 within uncertainties (PDG 2024 review).

nodes.label: Fermion masses m_{e}, m_{μ}, m_{u}, m_{d}

extra.sub: parameters · fix the Yukawa couplings y_{f}
extra.desc: The SM explains the mechanism of fermion mass but not the values: each mass fixes one Yukawa coupling. Calibration edges.
Di-Higgs production has not been observed; current limits constrain λ_{HHH}/λ_{SM} to roughly a window of order unity around the SM value (ATLAS/CMS, Run 2). A prediction awaiting its observable.

Atmospheric ν_{μ} disappearance (Super-Kamiokande 1998), solar ν flavour change (SNO 2002) and reactor ν̄_{e} disappearance (KamLAND 2003) require non-degenerate neutrino masses. In the graph as built the ν sectors are massless (no right-handed state), so no Yukawa node reaches them: in-degree zero from the model layer.
